title: The proper bowl
translation: The Koga Chancellor once asked for water in the courtiers' hall at the palace. The woman on duty brought it in a plain clay cup. "Bring the proper bowl," he said, and he drank from that.
original: {久我|こが}の{相国|しやうこく}は、{殿上|てんじやう}にて{水|みづ}を{召|め}しけるに、{主殿司|とのもりづかさ}{土器|どき}をたてまつりければ、
「まがりを{参|まゐ}らせよ。」とて、まがりしてぞめしける。
literal: When the Koga Chancellor asked for water in the courtiers' hall, the (woman of the) housekeeping office offered an earthenware cup,
(and) saying 'Bring a magari', he drank with a magari.

notes.text: {相国|しやうこく}: the chancellor (see section 99). He is usually identified as Koga Michimitsu (1187–1248), but commentators do not all agree.
{殿上|てんじやう}: the courtiers' hall in the emperor's residence, where nobles of high enough rank waited and met. Being allowed in was a privilege in itself.
{主殿司|とのもりづかさ}: one of the offices of women who served in the palace, in charge of lamps, fuel and cleaning. Readings vary (とのもづかさ is also found).
An unglazed clay cup, the cheap kind that was used once and thrown away, mostly for sake. It is usually read かはらけ; the 1925 edition gives どき, which this page keeps.

What exactly a まがり was is not certain. Most commentators take it as a bowl, probably of metal or bent wood, that was the correct vessel for water in the courtiers' hall. The translation says 'the proper bowl' for that reason.

notes.quote: まがりしてぞめしける
notes.text: ぞ … ける: ぞ needs the attributive form, so けり becomes ける. {召|め}す: here 'to drink' (respectful). Kenkō tells the story and stops. Like section 99, it is a story about court precedent.
